episode_title: Can We Build Switzerland in India?

stories.topic: The young man who wants to stay in Himachal
stories.summary: The crew held an Everything is Everything viewers' meetup in Bir, and only a couple of people came at short notice. One was Shubham Dhiman, who drove three hours from his village near Hamirpur. He had done the public policy course at Takshashila and was full of curiosity about policy, yet rooted in the place: he didn't want a city job, he wanted to do something for Himachal. His conversation with Ajay raised the question of how to develop such places without destroying them, and that question became this episode.
stories.insight: The scarce input for local development is curious, policy-literate people who choose to stay. The episode is partly a toolkit addressed to them.
stories.quote: He says I don't want to go and work in a city, I want to do something for Himachal, which we absolutely loved.

stories.topic: How Udaipur bet on its lakes over farming
stories.summary: Udaipur's lakes used to depend on the monsoon. In good years the city was staggeringly beautiful. In other years the water evaporated, and people would check with each other whether 'the lakes are nice' before deciding to go. Vasundhara Raje, Rajiv Mehrishi and others then changed Rajasthan's rules for prioritising irrigation water: whatever the scarcity, Udaipur's lakes get water first. Farmers lower in the queue lost out in the short term. But Udaipur became a high-value tourism engine, the 'Venice of the East', and lakhs of livelihoods now connect to its economy.
stories.insight: One deliberate trade-off, based on which use of a scarce resource creates more value, can change a region's destiny. Rajasthan is not great farmland, so it stopped playing a B-grade agriculture game and went world-class on the asset it uniquely had.
stories.quote: Whatever be the scarcity of water, first, Udaipur lakes will get water. Why? Because it's a trivial calculation that the resource flows you get out of tourism are just staggeringly large compared to the income from agriculture.

stories.topic: Abandoned villages, from Uttarakhand to the Sahyadris
stories.summary: Uttarakhand has more than 3,000 abandoned villages. On the way up to Panchachuli, Ajay stayed in a village of about 200 houses with only three families left, and each hiker was offered an entire empty house for the night. On the Pindari Glacier trek he heard about a pregnant woman whom four men carried 20 km on a stretcher to reach the nearest health facility. Leaving such places is rational. He now sees the same thing in the deep Sahyadris: on a nine-day trek in January (the one where he broke his ankle on day five), he reached a village on day three with about twenty houses and just one old man and one old woman still living there.
stories.insight: The old picture of Himalayan development as a fight between too many people and the forests is out of date. Low fertility and out-migration mean remote India is emptying out, and policy has to start from that fact.
stories.quote: And there were three families living there. Meaning there were about 197 empty houses.

stories.summary: Dharamshala began with the Dalai Lama's arrival in 1959 and an airport soon after. Its fame spread slowly, by word of mouth and the Lonely Planet. By the 1980s it had become overcrowded, with all the failures of a bad Indian city. High-value tourists moved up to McLeod Ganj, which worked for about twenty years before it too went bad. They then moved to Lower Dharamkot, which degraded in turn, and then to Upper Dharamkot. Now Dharamshala has become a cricket venue, and Ajay predicts the low-value crowds that come with cricket will soon destroy Upper Dharamkot too.
stories.insight: Without urban governance, decline repeats as a series of steps. Each place enjoys a 20–30 year bloom, gets ruined by negative externalities, and the high-value visitors move further uphill. For Ajay, watching this happen was the moment he understood the problem.
stories.quote: And cricket unfortunately goes with very low value tourists.

stories.topic: Looking down at Bir through smoke from Billing
stories.summary: The day before recording, the crew stood at Billing, 2,500 metres up, and looked down at Bir 800 metres below. The town was covered in a haze of particulate matter from fires, including tourists' bonfires. From the landing ground below, you could barely see Billing. Ajay's fix: drones with thermal cameras to spot every fire, and a policeman sent to fine whoever lit it ten thousand rupees.
stories.insight: Clean air and a clear view are public goods, and a bonfire is a textbook negative externality. No individual can fix it, so this is exactly where even a freedom-first thinker says the state must act.
stories.quote: Everybody's view is damaged when you are standing at the landing ground, you can barely see Billing because we are just in a haze of solid particulate matter where people are burning stuff.

stories.topic: The book fair that made a hiker
stories.summary: At about eleven, Ajay wandered into a book fair in Bombay and found Harish Kapadia's Trek the Sahyadris. He read it a hundred times. Then, with no help and no knowledge, he and a group of other kids from Bandra East started hiking in the Sahyadris on their own.
stories.insight: One book found by chance at the right age can shape a whole life. Amit then turns this around and suggests Ajay can now be that spark for young people.
stories.quote: So thank you, Harish Kapadia, you changed my life.

recommendations.creator: Alain Bertaud
recommendations.context: Amit's first pick in the closing recommendations, tied to the episode's discussion of town planning.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a masterpiece and a desert-island book. It is about more than town planning: it shows how urban planning and economics come together, with many good frameworks for thinking about cities.

recommendations.creator: Barry Lopez
recommendations.context: Amit's second pick, prompted by being surrounded by the landscape around Bir.
recommendations.reason: Lopez is one of the great travel writers and a beautiful, introspective writer. Amit says a journey becomes truly beautiful when it is also a journey inside you.

recommendations.creator: Harish Kapadia
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation, told through the story of finding it at a Bombay book fair at about age eleven.
recommendations.reason: It was a turning point in his life. He read it a hundred times, and it started his lifelong hiking in the Sahyadris.

recommendations.creator: Harish Kapadia
recommendations.context: Kapadia's new book from 2023, recommended right after Ajay's tribute to him.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it a lovely book and essential if you take an interest in the Himalayas.

recommendations.creator: Malini Goyal and Prashanth Prakash
recommendations.context: Raised during the Bir-versus-Bangalore discussion of urban governance.
recommendations.reason: Its line that Bangalore's software is 5G but its hardware is 2G captures the city's governance failure. Amit uses it to argue that in Bir the hardware is the product.

recommendations.item: Malini Goyal is the Curious One (Episode 377 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'a great episode' while bringing up Malini Goyal's book on Bangalore.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation with the journalist behind the 5G-software, 2G-hardware diagnosis of Bangalore.

recommendations.item: Pritika Hingorani Wants to Fix Our Cities (Episode 361 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Ajay notes there are 'many, many great Seen and the Unseen episodes' on urban policy, and names Pritika Hingorani as someone whose expertise towns like Bir should draw on.
recommendations.reason: Background on the urban governance knowledge that Ajay says can carry straight over to Himalayan towns.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay cites its chapter title 'you must learn to walk before you can run' when arguing that urban reformers should start with small towns.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of the policy principle behind his case for fixing Bir before Bangalore: begin with smaller, solvable problems.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers to their earlier agriculture episode while explaining why the usual plains recipe doesn't fit the Himalayas.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the case for market-based agriculture, the standard recipe this episode contrasts with a Himalaya-specific strategy.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay connects the abandoned-villages story to 'conversations we've had around population as a problem.'
recommendations.reason: Background on India's changing demographic transition, which shapes the strategy for the Himalayan states.

recommendations.item: The Hiking Episode (Episode 35 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's closing line, after Ajay's tribute to Harish Kapadia.
recommendations.reason: Amit suggests Ajay can be for young people what Kapadia was for him, so he asks viewers to watch the hiking episode.

recommendations.creator: Takshashila Institution
recommendations.context: Mentioned while introducing Shubham Dhiman, who had done the Takshashila public policy course.
recommendations.reason: Shubham, a policy-curious young Himachali who inspired the episode, came through this course.

core_ideas.concept: Development for the locals, not scenery for the visitors
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay rejects the outsider's wish that hill people stay poor so their places stay pretty. The goal is sustained economic growth for the people of the Himalayan states, and the only question is which strategy delivers it. Amit adds that worrying about 'low-value tourism' is not snobbery. The test is whether locals prosper while the place keeps what makes it good, and the low-level equilibrium fails both: locals earn less and the beauty is destroyed.
core_ideas.quote: So sometimes there is an outsiders condescending view that we want you to live at low levels of income because we would like your places to be nice for us. And I'm not there at all.

core_ideas.concept: The plains recipe fails in the mountains
core_ideas.explanation: The usual path for states like Gujarat or Haryana is infrastructure, factories and modern agriculture. It doesn't transfer to the Himalayas. These states are landlocked, so they lack the coastline that gives cheap access to container ships and world trade. Mountain airports, railways and highways are hugely expensive and would need very high user charges. Following the standard recipe means always doing it worse than the plains. In line with the subsidiarity principle, the local political system should pick its own priorities.
core_ideas.quote: The airports, the highways, the railway lines in these states will always be 50% inferior to what is done in the plains.

core_ideas.explanation: Udaipur has its lakes; the Himalayan states have the Himalayas. Switzerland, Colorado and Japan show that a beautiful place can support a high-value tourism economy and first-world incomes for locals over generations. The strategy should be built around that unique asset.
core_ideas.quote: There is only one Himalayas in the entire planet Earth.

core_ideas.explanation: Fertility rates in Himachal and Uttarakhand are around 1.6–1.7, with similar levels in Sikkim and Bhutan. Together with out-migration, this points to gently declining populations and thousands of abandoned villages. The 1950s–60s worry about people clearing forests for farms and houses no longer applies, and tourism's low use of labour is no longer a problem.
core_ideas.quote: So the age of rapid population growth is over, in fact.

core_ideas.concept: Freedom first, then market failure, then the state
core_ideas.explanation: The disciplined public-economics method: start by imagining the world where people do whatever they want, and respect the creativity and bottom-up energy in society. Then find what goes wrong, classify it as a market failure, and only then ask whether the state can uniquely add value.
core_ideas.quote: Start at the baseline, freedom is normal, people will do whatever they want.

core_ideas.concept: Tourism GDP = N × P, and externalities wreck P
core_ideas.explanation: A region's tourism income is the number of tourists (N) times their daily spend (P). Left alone, each establishment rationally adds disco lights, loudspeakers and bonfires to attract customers, but each one spoils the area around it. These uncoordinated choices push out high-spending visitors. Chasing N lowers P.
core_ideas.quote: They've just destroyed a circle with a radius of two hundred meters surrounding themselves.

core_ideas.concept: The boom-bust trap and the hundred-year view
core_ideas.explanation: A place gets 20–30 good years, then collapses into a stable low-income equilibrium. Low-value tourists don't require high human capital to serve them, and they degrade the place further, a vicious cycle. Sustainability here means an economic arc that keeps rising over a century, the timescale on which human capital and a 'Switzerland of India' get built. There are no quick fixes.
core_ideas.quote: You get brief growth, it goes away. You get brief growth, it goes away.

core_ideas.concept: Town planning as lines on maps, not micromanagement
core_ideas.explanation: Following Bimal Patel, about 40–50% of land should be marked for streets and parks before unplanned construction makes that impossible. This answers Amit's worry about high modernism. Ajay rejects the Indian style of planning that specifies every school and petrol pump, but argues that basic rule of law alone can't handle urban market failures. In Bir, he imagines a vehicle-free walking zone with cafés across from the paragliding landing ground.
core_ideas.quote: But the foundations that Bimal Patel has emphasized is you are stuck if you don't have that forty, fifty percent of the land allocated to the streets and the parks.

core_ideas.concept: Why Bir is a better bet than Bangalore
core_ideas.explanation: This is Ajay's answer to Amit's worry about isomorphic mimicry. First, small towns are easier to fix, so urban reformers should learn there before taking on big cities. Second, incentives line up. Bangalore sells software, so residents complain about the city but tolerate it, and the state becomes predatory, extracting money from the software makers. Bir sells the place itself, so good governance and income move together. Udaipur shows the effect: locals keep it clean, and police treat a woman's safety at 2 AM as make-or-break. He also says the knowledge comes first: reach out to the frontier experts instead of accepting normal Indian town planning, and learn from community successes he cites in Meghalaya, Bhutan and Nepal.
core_ideas.quote: So in Bangalore, people are much more casual about littering because their business is software.

core_ideas.explanation: Kangra's runway is around 1,300 m and Kullu's around 1,100 m, too short for big aircraft. Ladakh shows the logic: because you must fly to Delhi and then to Leh, the effort involved selects for a different, higher-value tourist than easy road access does. Longer runways would shift Himachal's visitor mix upward.

Indian parks stop poaching and commercial development, which is good, but they contribute almost nothing to GDP. Yellowstone gets about four million visitors a year spending $1,000–2,000 each, which Ajay puts at $4–8 billion in revenue, and it has about 900 miles of trails. The model for places like the Great Himalayan National Park: attractive gateway villages like Bir on the edge, hundreds of kilometres of walking trails, campgrounds, and a little high-end lodging run by private operators under strict biodiversity contracts. He adds that Sikkim's Kangchenjunga reserve, about 2,000 of the state's 7,000 sq km, could be run jointly with Nepal's matching reserve.
core_ideas.quote: We've not yet figured out how to contribute to the GDP.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the hypocrisy of complaining about crowds: 'the definition of too many tourists is a tourist who comes after me.'
Amit admits that while listening to Ajay talk with Shubham, his first thought was 'episode!' Then he corrects himself: the proper phrase is 'knowledge to the world', not talk of churning out content.
Ajay's picture of an unmanaged Bir: five restaurants competing with 'five thousand watts and ten thousand watts' and lights 'blinking so that the aliens can see us from Alpha Centauri.'

Amit, after Ajay's jab at cricket crowds: 'If there are any cricket people watching this, kindly excuse, we love you, I love you, we love cricket. All cricket people are not the same, we contain multitudes.'
Ajay's offer to viewers: 'if you ask us in triplicate, we will give you the latitude and longitude of the location where each session was recorded.'
Amit stopping his own reflection on inner journeys: '...sounding like a pop philosopher. Enough of this.'
Steven Pinker's 'nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them', which Amit applies to regions: each place has different natural knobs, so policy has to fit them.
John Maynard Keynes: after starting from freedom and identifying market failures, Ajay says, 'we would start like John Maynard Keynes and wonder' whether the state can add value.
Dire Straits' 'Telegraph Road' from Love Over Gold, the song Ajay thinks of as he describes a pristine place being discovered by Instagrammers and YouTubers and then built over.

The show's origin: at the Emergent Ventures conference in Udaipur, by a lake a year before launch, the hosts came up with two names: 'Watching the Wheels', after a John Lennon song, and 'Everything is Everything', which Amit attributes to a Bruce Springsteen song.
Malini Goyal's line on Bangalore: 'the software is 5G, but the hardware is 2G.' Amit adds that in Bir the software is the hardware and needs to be made 5G.
Ajay calls Udaipur 'the Venice of the East', one of the most beautiful cities in the world, built on high-value tourism.
'You must learn to walk before you can run', a chapter title from Kelkar and Shah's In Service of the Republic, used to argue that urban reformers should start with small towns.
